organizingIdeas.title: Number
organizingIdeas.statement: Quantity is measured with numbers that enable counting, labelling, comparing, and operating.

guidingQuestions.question: How can place value support organization of number?

knowledge.text: For numbers in base-10, each place has 10 times the value of the place to its right.
The digits 0 to 9 indicate the number of groups in each place in a number.
The value of each place in a number is the product of the digit and its place value.
Numbers can be composed in various ways by using place value.
Numbers can be rounded in contexts where an exact count is not needed.
The less than sign, <, and the greater than sign, >, are used to show the relationship between two unequal numbers.
A zero in the leftmost place of a natural number does not change the value of the number.
The dollar sign, $, is placed to the left of the dollar value in English and to the right of the dollar value in French.
The cent sign, ¢, is placed to the right of the cent value in English and in French.

understanding.text: Place value is the basis for the base-10 system.
Place value determines the value of a digit based on its place in a number relative to the ones place.
Place value is used to read, write, and compare numbers.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify the place value of each digit in a natural number.
Relate the values of adjacent places.
Determine the value of each digit in a natural number.
Express natural numbers, using words and numerals.
Express various compositions of a natural number, using place value.
Round natural numbers to various places.
Compare and order natural numbers.
Express the relationship between two numbers, using <, >, or =.
Count and represent the value of a collection of nickels, dimes, and quarters as cents.
Count and represent the value of a collection of loonies, toonies, and bills as dollars.
Recognize French and English symbolic representations of monetary values.

guidingQuestions.question: How can processes be established for addition and subtraction?

outcomes.outcome: Students apply strategies for addition and subtraction within 1000.

knowledge.text: Recall of addition and subtraction number facts facilitates addition and subtraction strategies.
Standard algorithms for addition and subtraction are conventional procedures based on place value.
Estimation can be used to support addition and subtraction in everyday situations, including
items: when an exact sum or difference is not needed
to check if an answer is reasonable

understanding.text: Addition and subtraction strategies can be chosen based on the nature of the numbers.
Standard algorithms for addition and subtraction may be used for any natural numbers.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Relate strategies for the addition and subtraction of two-digit numbers to strategies for the addition and subtraction of three-digit numbers.
Model regrouping by place value for addition and subtraction.
Explain the standard algorithms for addition and subtraction of natural numbers.
Add and subtract natural numbers, using standard algorithms.
Estimate sums and differences.
Solve problems, using addition and subtraction.

guidingQuestions.question: How can multiplication and division provide new perspectives of number?

outcomes.outcome: Students analyze and apply strategies for multiplication and division within 100.

knowledge.text: Multiplication and division are inverse mathematical operations.
Multiplication can represent repeated addition.
Multiplication can be interpreted in various ways according to context, such as
Division can be interpreted in various ways according to context, such as
The order in which two quantities are multiplied does not affect the product (commutative property).
The order in which two numbers are divided affects the quotient.
Multiplication or division by 1 results in the same number (identity property).

understanding.text: Quantities can be composed and decomposed through multiplication and division.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Compose a product, using equal groups of objects.
Relate multiplication to repeated addition.
Relate multiplication to skip counting.
Investigate multiplication by 0.
Model a quotient by partitioning a quantity into equal groups or groups of a certain size, with or without remainders.
Visualize and model products and quotients as arrays.
Recognize interpretations of multiplication and division in various contexts.

knowledge.text: Numbers can be multiplied or divided in parts (distributive property).
Multiplication strategies include
Division strategies include
Products can be expressed symbolically by using the multiplication sign, \times, factors, and the equal sign.
Quotients can be expressed symbolically by using the division sign, \div, dividend, divisor, and the equal sign.
A missing quantity in a product or quotient can be represented in different ways, including
A remainder is the quantity left over after division.

understanding.text: Sharing and grouping situations can be interpreted as multiplication or division.
Multiplication and division strategies can be supported by addition and subtraction.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Investigate multiplication and division strategies.
Multiply numbers up to a product of 100 and divide numbers with a maximum dividend of 100.
Verify a product or quotient, using inverse operations.
Determine a missing quantity in a product or quotient in a variety of ways.
Express multiplication and division symbolically.
Explain the meaning of the remainder in various situations.
Solve problems, using multiplication and division in sharing or grouping situations.

knowledge.text: A multiplication table shows both multiplication and division facts.
Fact families are groups of related multiplication and division number facts.

understanding.text: Multiplication number facts have related division facts.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Examine patterns in multiplication and division, including patterns in multiplication tables and skip counting.
Recognize families of related multiplication and division number facts.
Recall multiplication number facts, with factors to 10, and related division facts.

guidingQuestions.question: How can fractions contribute to a sense of number?

outcomes.outcome: Students interpret fractions in relation to one whole.

knowledge.text: The same fraction can represent
items: equal parts of one whole length, shape, or object
equal groups of one whole quantity
equal parts of each equal group in one whole quantity

knowledge.text: The name of a fraction describes its composition as a number of unit fractions.
Fraction notation, (\frac{a}{b}), relates the numerator, a, a number of equal parts, to the denominator, b, the total number of equal parts in the whole.
Equal numerators or equal denominators can facilitate the comparison of fractions.
A fraction with a numerator that is equal to its denominator is one whole.
Each fraction is associated with a point on the number line.

understanding.text: Fractions are numbers between natural numbers.
Fractions can represent part-to-whole relationships.
A unit fraction describes the size of the equal parts of a fraction.
The size of the parts and the total number of equal parts in the whole are inversely related.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Model fractions of a whole quantity, length, shape, or object, in various ways, limited to denominators of 12 or less.
Visualize fractions as compositions of a unit fraction.
Identify the numerator and denominator of a fraction in various representations.
Name a given fraction.
Express fractions, including one whole, symbolically, limited to denominators of 12 or less.
Relate various representations of the same fraction, limited to denominators of 12 or less.
Compare the same fraction of different-sized wholes.
Compare different fractions of the same whole that have the same denominator.
Compare different fractions of the same whole that have the same numerator and different denominators.
Express the relationship between two fractions of the same whole, using <, >, or =.
Relate a fraction less than one to its position on the number line, limited to denominators of 12 or less.
Compare fractions to benchmarks of 0, \frac{1}{2}, and 1.

guidingQuestions.question: How can equality facilitate agility with number?

knowledge.text: An equation uses the equal sign to indicate equality between two expressions.
The left and right sides of an equation are interchangeable.

understanding.text: Two expressions are equal if they represent the same number.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Write equations that represent equality between a number and an expression or between two different expressions of the same number.

knowledge.text: Equations can be modelled by using a balance.
A symbol may represent an unknown value in an equation.

understanding.text: Equations can have unknown values.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Model equations that include an unknown value, including with a balance.
Determine an unknown value on the left or right side of an equation, limited to equations with one operation.
Solve problems, using equations, limited to equations with one operation.

organizingIdeas.title: Geometry
organizingIdeas.statement: Shapes are defined and related by geometric attributes.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways might geometric properties refine interpretation of shape?

outcomes.outcome: Students relate geometric properties to shape.

knowledge.text: Geometric properties can describe relationships, including perpendicular, parallel, and equal.
Parallel lines or planes are always the same distance apart.
Perpendicular lines or planes intersect at a 90° (right) angle.
Right angles can be identified by using various referents, such as
items: the corner of a piece of paper
the angle between the hands on an analog clock at 3:00

knowledge.text: Polygons include
Regular polygons have sides of equal length and interior angles of equal measure.

understanding.text: Geometric properties are relationships between geometric attributes.
Geometric properties define a class of polygon.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Investigate the relationships between the sides of a polygon, including perpendicular, parallel, and equal, using referents for 90° or by measuring.
Investigate the relationships between vertices of a polygon, including equal or right angles, using direct comparison or referents for 90°.
Describe geometric properties of regular and irregular polygons.
Sort polygons according to geometric properties and describe the sorting rule.
Classify polygons as regular or irregular, using geometric properties.

knowledge.text: Transformations include
The distance between any two vertices of a shape is maintained in the image created by a transformation.

understanding.text: Geometric properties do not change when a polygon undergoes a transformation.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Examine geometric properties of polygons by translating, rotating, or reflecting, using hands-on materials or digital applications.

organizingIdeas.title: Measurement
organizingIdeas.statement: Attributes such as length, area, volume, and angle are quantified by measurement.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can length be communicated?

outcomes.outcome: Students determine length, using standard units.

knowledge.text: The basic unit of length in the metric system is the metre.
Metric units are named by using prefixes that indicate the relationship to the basic unit, including
items: milli: one thousand millimetres in one metre
centi: one hundred centimetres in one metre
deci: ten decimetres in one metre

knowledge.text: Metric units are abbreviated for convenience, including
Standard measuring tools show iterations of a standard unit from an origin.
Units of length in the imperial system include inch, foot, and yard, related in these ways:
Approximate conversions between metric and imperial are useful in real-world situations, including

understanding.text: Length is measured in standard units according to the metric system and the imperial system.
Length can be expressed in various units according to context and desired precision.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Relate millimetres, centimetres, and metres.
Relate inches to feet and yards.
Justify the choice of millimetres, centimetres, or metres to measure various lengths.
Measure lengths of straight lines and curves, with millimetres, centimetres, or metres.
Recognize length expressed in metric or imperial units.
Approximate a measurement in inches, feet, or yards, using centimetres or metres.

knowledge.text: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides.

understanding.text: Length remains the same when decomposed or rearranged.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Determine the perimeter of polygons.
Determine the length of an unknown side, given the perimeter of a polygon.

knowledge.text: A benchmark is a known length to which another length can be compared.
Length can be estimated by using a personal or familiar referent.

understanding.text: Length can be estimated when less accuracy is required.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify referents for a centimetre and a metre.
Estimate length by comparing to a benchmark.
Estimate length by visualizing the iteration of a referent for a centimetre or metre.

guidingQuestions.question: How can angles broaden an understanding of space?

knowledge.text: Angle defines the space in
The arms of an angle can be line segments or rays.
A vertex is the common end point of two arms.

understanding.text: An angle is formed when two arms meet at a vertex.
An angle can be interpreted as the motion of a length rotated about a vertex.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize various angles in surroundings.
Recognize situations in which an angle can be perceived as motion.

knowledge.text: Superimposing is the process of placing one angle over another to compare angles.
A referent is a personal or familiar representation of a known angle.

understanding.text: Two angles can be compared directly or indirectly.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Compare two angles directly by superimposing.
Compare two angles indirectly by superimposing a third angle.
Estimate which of two angles is greater.
Identify referents for 90°.
Identify 90° angles in the environment, using a referent.

organizingIdeas.title: Patterns
organizingIdeas.statement: Awareness of patterns supports problem solving in various situations.

guidingQuestions.question: How can diverse representations of patterns contribute to interpretation of change?

outcomes.outcome: Students analyze patterns in numerical sequences.

knowledge.text: Ordinal numbers can indicate position in a sequence.
Finite sequences, such as a countdown, have a definite end.
Infinite sequences, such as the natural numbers, never end.

understanding.text: A sequence is a list of terms arranged in a certain order.
Sequences may be finite or infinite.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize familiar numerical sequences, including the sequence of even or odd numbers.
Describe position in a sequence, using ordinal numbers.
Differentiate between finite and infinite sequences.

knowledge.text: Numerical sequences can be constructed by using addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division.

understanding.text: A sequence can progress according to a pattern.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize skip-counting sequences in various representations, including rows or columns of a multiplication table.
Determine any missing term in a skip-counting sequence, using multiplication.
Describe the change from term to term in a numerical sequence, using mathematical operations.

organizingIdeas.title: Time
organizingIdeas.statement: Duration is described and quantified by time.

knowledge.text: Clocks relate seconds to minutes and hours according to a base-60 system.
The basic unit of time is the second.
One second is \frac{1}{60} of a minute.
One minute is \frac{1}{60} of an hour.
Analog and digital clocks represent time of day.
Time of day can be expressed as a duration relative to 12:00 in two 12-hour cycles.
Time of day can be expressed as a duration relative to 0:00 in one 24-hour cycle in some contexts, including French-language contexts.

understanding.text: Clocks are standard measuring tools used to communicate time.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Investigate relationships between seconds, minutes, and hours, using an analog clock.
Relate minutes past the hour to minutes until the next hour.
Describe time of day as a.m. or p.m. relative to 12-hour cycles of day and night.
Tell time, using analog and digital clocks.
Express time of day in relation to one 24-hour cycle.

organizingIdeas.title: Statistics
organizingIdeas.statement: The science of collecting, analyzing, visualizing, and interpreting data can inform understanding and decision making.

outcomes.outcome: Students interpret and explain representations of data.

knowledge.text: Statistical questions are questions that can be answered by collecting data.

understanding.text: Representation connects data to a statistical question.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Formulate statistical questions for investigation.
Predict the answer to a statistical question.

knowledge.text: First-hand data is collected by the person using the data.
Second-hand data is data collected by others from sources such as websites and social media.

understanding.text: Representation expresses data specific to a unique time and place.
Representation tells a story about data.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Collect data, using digital or non-digital tools and resources.
Represent first-hand and second-hand data in a dot plot or bar graph with one-to-one correspondence.
Describe the story that a representation tells about a collection of data in relation to a statistical question.
Examine First Nations, Métis, or Inuit representations of data.
Consider possible answers to a statistical question based on the data collected.
